Stop building a bot team on day one!

It's the most common overcomplication I see with Grok Bot. Someone wants help with their home finances, so they set up a bills bot, a subscriptions bot, a budget bot and a reminders bot. Four bots, four sets of instructions, lots of handoffs, and a token bill to match.

Here's what works better: one topic, one bot.

One money bot can find your subscriptions, flag the ones you don't use, remind you before bills are due, and give you a weekly summary. It sees the whole picture, so it connects things four separate bots would miss.

Why one bot works better at the start:

- It keeps all the context. Nothing gets lost between bots.
- Fewer handoffs means fewer tokens.
- You only fix one set of instructions when something's off.
- Most "new bots" are really just a new prompt or routine for the bot you already have.

So when does a second bot make sense? When the work becomes a genuinely different job: a different topic, different tools, or a different audience. Your money bot shouldn't also plan your meals.

Start with one bot per topic. Let it own everything about that topic. Split only when it hurts.

Grok Bot tip: give your busy bot a helper.

My DNA bot, Helix, kept hitting the same wall. Each bot gets one browser, so when Helix was busy on one site, everything else had to wait in line. That ate up a lot of time.

So I built Strand, a second bot whose whole job is to help Helix. Anything that needs a visual look in a browser, Strand can take while Helix keeps looking at something else. Strand can also run its own background tasks, so Helix gets more work done at once. No more waiting in line.

If one of your bots keeps stalling while it waits its turn, give it a teammate.

note_tweet.text:
Cua (30.4k GitHub stars, YC S25) just dropped the Cua Spaces SDK with a bold pitch: "Every big lab ships a bot with its own computer. None let you bring your own. Now you can."

What they didn’t put in the headline is the wildest part of the story.

Just 24 hours before launching this SDK, this 3-person team quietly killed their own cloud service (Cua Cloud). They realized fighting E2B, Daytona, and Modal on server margins is a suicide mission. So overnight, they turned their former rivals into backend suppliers and pivoted into the "universal remote control" for AI agents.

A deep dive into the pain points, the moat, the crazy vision, and the fatal flaw behind Cua Spaces:

1/ Brain-Body Decoupling

Strip away the "Computer-Use 2.0" hype, and Cua Spaces is basically TeamViewer + Vagrant + AutoHotkey built for AI agents.

Right now, Grok Bot, Meta’s Muse, and OpenAI’s dots lock their agents inside their own closed cloud computers. Those sandboxes are pricey, locked to one model, and completely empty, none of your local files, internal network access, or active logins are there.

Cua separates the brain (Claude Code, Codex, Gemini CLI) from the body (your laptop, an idle Mac mini, AWS, or a Daytona/Modal sandbox). You test a bot locally, change on: "local" to on: "office-mac-mini", and the exact same code runs on another machine.

2/ Fixing the Two Biggest Headaches of Local Agents

Anyone who has tried running GUI agents locally knows two instant dealbreakers: the bot hijacks your mouse so you can't work, and cloud sandboxes immediately get blocked by Cloudflare captchas and 2FA logins.

Cua solved both with surprisingly slick engineering:

> Multiplayer & Background Clicks
Their underlying cua-driver sends clicks and keystrokes directly to background windows without stealing focus. You and the agent get separate cursors on the same screen.

> Teleport (Air-dropping Logins)
On a Mac, you literally drag a logged-in Chrome or Slack window up into your screen's notch, and Cua packages the active session and drops it straight into the isolated sandbox. No re-logging in, and the agent never sees your raw password.

3/ Doing the Dirty Work on macOS

Why won’t big model labs or Linux sandbox startups crush them?

Because almost everyone else only builds for Linux containers, while Cua conquered macOS. Virtualizing macOS is a nightmare of Apple TCC permission popups, strict kernel limits, and dropped keystrokes. Cua built Lume (a high-speed Apple Silicon virtualization engine) and cua-driver, infrastructure so solid that even rival open-source projects like OpenMausBot use Cua’s driver under the hood.

They also played a clever licensing game: the low-level drivers are MIT licensed to win 30k+ developer stars, while the new Spaces desktop and iOS apps are locked under FSL (Functional Source License), meaning you can read the code, but competitors can’t legally host or resell it.

4/ Cyber-Foreman & Apple Legal Jiu-Jitsu

While the rest of Silicon Valley is busy writing MCP servers and APIs for agents, Cua’s philosophy is wonderfully unhinged: 90% of human software will never have good APIs, so just give every bot a screen and let it click buttons like a human.

With their open-source iOS app, the vision is turning you into a "cyber-foreman." You walk down the street watching ten Claude Codes operate ten different desktops from your iPhone. When a bot hits a login wall, you tap Face ID on your phone to approve the password injection and let it keep working.

Even smarter? Apple’s legal terms strictly forbid renting out macOS virtual machines at scale in the cloud. By shutting down their cloud and telling users to run Spaces on their own spare Mac minis, Cua neatly offloaded all the Apple EULA legal risk onto the end user's hardware.

5/ A Plaintext Relay & A Stretched Team

Before you plug your company's infrastructure into Cua, you need to know where the bodies are buried.

If you read Cua’s security documentation closely, they drop a massive bombshell: their official relay (https://t.co/uinqWXJRkG) is NOT end-to-end encrypted. It is a TLS-terminating proxy. Aside from sealed Teleport bundles, your shell outputs, transferred files, desktop video streams, and every single keystroke pass through their relay server’s memory in plaintext.

To their credit, they are brutally honest about it，publishing a doc titled "What the relay can see" that openly admits a relay breach would compromise every connected session. Add in the fact that a 3-person team is maintaining a Rust core, 4 OS drivers, and mobile apps (and just had to tell users to urgently uninstall their legacy cuabot package due to known security vulnerabilities), and you can see how thin the ice is.

6/ Cua Spaces is a masterclass in startup survival. They realized renting cloud VMs is a race to the bottom, so they pivoted to charging $18–$30/month for the control plane and remote streaming relay instead.

If you are an indie builder using Cua over a local network or your own private Tailscale mesh (bypassing their plaintext relay), it is easily one of the coolest agent tools on the market today. If you are an enterprise CISO, that default relay is an instant red flag until true E2EE leaves beta.

Would you trust an AI agent with its own background desktop on your personal Mac, or are you keeping your bots locked in the cloud?
